opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that once you move past a single request and response, everything gets harder. When you're running conversational AI at the scale we are, a lot of what actually happens isn't one model call. It's a chain of things: you pull context, maybe call a couple of models, run some safety or ranking step, write state back, maybe kick off something asynchronous. Any one of those steps can fail. A GPU node gets preempted, a downstream service times out, a deploy rolls through in the middle of a workflow.

Without durable execution, every team ends up hand-rolling the same fragile stuff: retry loops, idempotency keys, little state machines in a database, cron jobs that sweep up whatever got stuck. It works until it doesn't, and when it breaks it's really painful to debug because the state of the workflow is spread across logs and tables and people's heads.

So for us it's foundational because it's the layer that lets everything else be simple. If I can write a workflow as ordinary code and know that if the process dies halfway through, it picks up exactly where it left off, with the completed steps not re-run and the side effects not duplicated, then the engineers building product features don't have to think about failure modes constantly. They can just think about the logic.

And it matters even more as things get more agentic. When a workflow might run for minutes or hours, wait on a user, call tools, branch, you can't treat it as a stateless request anymore. You need something that treats the execution itself as a durable object you can inspect, replay, and recover. For a small team trying to move fast on a lot of traffic, getting that right once, at the infrastructure level, pays off in basically every feature we ship afterward.

r001.rationale: The response explains that retries, idempotency, state tracking, and recovery for failures create substantial engineering work around multi-step workflows.

r002.rationale: It discusses durable execution generally but does not identify Temporal as the way to run side effects or obtain retries without custom queue logic.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention biology or making it more like engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that it started as a pain point and turned into a thesis.

At Chai, the thing we actually ship is agents that run for a long time. Not a chat turn, not a single tool call, but a workflow that might take minutes or hours. It calls models, it calls tools, it waits on a human, it retries something that flaked, and then it has to pick up exactly where it left off. And the moment you have that shape, you've got a distributed systems problem whether you wanted one or not.

What we kept running into was that the hard part was never the model. The model is a function call. The hard part was everything around it. A pod gets evicted halfway through step eleven. A rate limit hits. The user closes the tab and comes back tomorrow. In a naive system, you've either lost the whole run, or you replay it from scratch and now you're paying for the same tokens twice and maybe double-charging a card or double-sending an email because a side effect ran again.

So durable execution, to me, is the abstraction that says: the state of this long-running thing lives somewhere that survives the process. Every step is recorded. If you crash, you resume from the log, not from zero. Side effects are idempotent or they're guarded. And crucially, the application developer writes it like straight-line code. They don't hand-roll a state machine with a database table of "current_step" and a cron job poking it.

I think it's foundational for two reasons. First, correctness. An agent that nondeterministically loses work is not a product, it's a demo. Second, and this is the one people underrate, it changes what you can build. Once a run can pause for a week waiting on a human approval and resume cheaply, you start designing agents that are supposed to be slow and careful. You stop fighting the runtime and start leaning on it.

And frankly, it moved us from treating reliability as something the infra team bolts on afterward to treating it as the substrate. That's why I call it foundational. Everything else at Chai sits on top of the assumption that a workflow, once started, will finish.

r001.rationale: The response says the model is a function call while the hard part is handling failures, retries, recovery, and duplicated side effects in distributed workflows.

r002.rationale: It describes retries and avoiding custom state-machine infrastructure, but does not identify Temporal as the way to achieve this.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss biology or reliable engineering primitives as a bottleneck to engineering biology.

astra-6.text:
I think once you build an application around models, you’re dealing with work that doesn’t fit neatly into a single request and response. You might call a model, use its output to call a tool, wait for something else, and then continue. Any one of those steps can fail, and some of them can take a long time.

The foundational question is: if a process dies halfway through, what happens to the work? Do you start over? Did a tool already perform an action that you’re now going to repeat? Can you recover without losing the context you’ve built up?

Durable execution gives you a way to make that progress persistent and recoverable. It doesn’t magically make every external action safe to retry—you still have to think about idempotency—but it gives you a place to manage those guarantees.

For Chai, I see that as foundational because otherwise every feature ends up solving its own version of retries, checkpoints, and recovery. You want engineers to focus on what the application should do, with a reliable foundation for making sure that work actually gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says steps can fail and features otherwise need their own retry and recovery solutions, but does not say failure handling can dominate the effort for a simple distributed computation.

r002.rationale: It discusses durable execution and retries generally, but does not identify running side effects through Temporal or getting retries without custom queue logic.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss biology or making it more like engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
Because once you have an AI system doing real work, you have to deal with the fact that the work can outlive any individual process. You’re calling a model, waiting on an external service, maybe waiting for a person to approve something. And somewhere in that sequence, a machine is going to restart or a request is going to time out.

The hard part isn’t just retrying. It’s knowing what already happened. Did that operation fail, or did it succeed and we just never get the response? Can we resume without repeating a side effect or throwing away all the work we’ve already done?

For Chai, that’s foundational because we don’t want every application to have to solve those questions independently with queues, database flags, and a bunch of recovery logic. Durable execution gives you a way to preserve progress and recover predictably. It doesn’t make the model deterministic or every external operation safe to retry, but it gives you a reliable foundation around those things. Then you can spend your time on what the system should do.
